extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Tatler / urban literate gentry interested in manners, letter-writing, and conduct
extracted.subtask_short: Tatler essays on manners and letters
extracted.subtask_description: Short prescriptive essays on upbringing, social conduct, letter-writing, and courtship for early-18th-century gentlemen and the polite public; mixes examples, anecdotes, and maxims about behaviour. Primarily advice for how to educate children, address women, behave in company, and observe decorum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match education and placement to a child's temperament
rubrics_metrics.description: Be particularly observant of the temper and inclinations of childhood and youth; what great evils or benefits arise from putting us in our tender years to what we are fit, or unfit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sound children's inclinations by showing them the town and entertainments; then assign them to stations suited to their natural make: a plodding child (Jack) should be trained for trade/citizenship to be the family's refuge; an arrogant bright lad (Will) sent to Oxford so raillery will expose coxcombry; a subtle, well-fashioned youth placed as a page to a great lady to learn courtly demeanour. Examples in text illustrate placing children where their temper will best serve family interests and future success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good breeding carries further than mere learning
rubrics_metrics.description: A good mien in a Court will carry a man greater lengths than a good understanding in any other place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: ceremony was invented to keep fools at a distance; good breeding equalises fools and wise men. Practical implication: invest in social manners and comportment (courtly behaviour, graceful manner) because these often outstrip academic or intellectual accomplishments in social advancement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Letter-writing: be as near to speech as possible
rubrics_metrics.description: There was no rule in the world to be made for writing letters, but that of being as near what you speak face to face as you can; writing has lost more mistresses than any one mistake in the whole legend of love.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid making love-letters overly plaintive or complaint-filled; do not display that 'the whole relish of his life depends upon her.' Instead, be pleasant and diverting: 'If possible therefore divert your mistress, rather than sigh to her.' Use natural, conversational tone; examples contrast Careless (negligent, diverting) with the serious Constant (solemn, affecting pity) to show which wins affection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer live charm and conviviality to printed wit
rubrics_metrics.description: Small appearance the prettiest things said in company make when in print.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The liveliness and context of conversation rarely translate to print; witty repartee and the effect of company often lose force on the page. Do not rely on printed accounts to reproduce the full value of social talk — cultivate in-person manners and quickness of repartee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courting a 'Platonne' (intellectual/platonic woman): silent consent, subtle flattery
rubrics_metrics.description: A Platonne is not to be touched with panegyric: she will tell you, it is a sensuality in the soul to be delighted that way. You are not therefore to commend, but silently consent to all she does, and says.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General flattery works for women in general, but with a Platonne avoid gross praise and overt panegyric; instead adopt silent assent and respectful veneration. Use subtlety, dissimulation, and demonstrated reverence for her intellectual posture rather than direct compliments or demonstrative physical passion; anecdote of Rake and the would-be Protestant nunnery shows how measured civility and feigned reverence can disarm or gain access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish conversational substance from mere brisk talk
rubrics_metrics.description: The prettiest company (quick, talkative) may be silly; the quieter companion who talks less often may show more understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In evaluating company prefer sly seriousness and home truths to brisk superficial witticisms. Example: Mistress Giddy (quick-tongued, common things) vs Mrs. Slim (speaks less but with understanding); practical conversational tactics include concise repartee and listening to create better company.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe public decorum in dress and behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: Notice that dress without regard to decorum (e.g., blue and red stockings in mourning; tucked cravats, and nightcap wigs, before people of the first quality) is unacceptable; compliance with demands for decorum is expected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public notices: those who flout established dress codes are urged to comply or leave. The periodical asserts social standards of appearance and threatens public rebuke; the principle is to conform outwardly to accepted modes of dress to avoid scandal or being excluded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatises and public arguments should demonstrate learning and reading
rubrics_metrics.description: It has been objected, that there is not learning, or much reading, shown therein, which is the very life and soul of all treatises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When defending or attacking customs (e.g., duelling), support arguments with learned authorities and citations; be open to admonition and consult learned persons or boards to reform errors. The narrator models consulting a 'learned board' when an objection about lack of learning is raised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure the degree of an affront before engaging in single combat
rubrics_metrics.description: I am forced to break off abruptly, being sent for in haste, with my rule, to measure the degree of an affront, before the two gentlemen... have made a pass.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical counsel (satirical) about duelling: assess provocation carefully, consider propriety and legal or social consequences, and weigh whether quarrel resolution by duel is warranted. The essay treats duelling with ironic legal/historical discussion, but endorses measured assessment of insults rather than immediate resort to violence.
